profile_summary.observed_hot_stack: mkh_user_main -> repeated mk_release -> ref_array_dispose -> repeated mk_release -> recursive object disposal/free
profile_summary.interpretation: Observed profile is weighted toward recursive managed-tree cleanup, with parseValue/parseString, ArrayList add/growth/read, allocation helpers and type/string access also visible. This is a profile sample, not an instrumentation count.

profile.profile_variant_change: Temporary copy of bench/json/json.kt with only REPS changed from 5 to 50 to hold the process long enough for a 3-second sample; generator/parser/walk logic and stdout checksum unchanged.

limitations: MK_STATS reports aggregate Mini managed-object allocation/free and reference-count events, not per-source callsite attribution; it does not count libc malloc/realloc from C helpers.
C handwritten reference uses malloc/realloc and has no existing MK_STATS hooks; no C allocator interposition was added.
Profile-only REPS=50 source is temporary and outside the repository; it repeats the same deterministic generator/parser/walk 50 times and matches REPS=5 stdout.
MK_STATS instrumented binaries are used for counts only; their elapsed time is not compared with normal timing.

handwritten_c_o3_reference_from_existing.caveat: Existing strict hand-C O3 data reused; bench/json/json.c and expected output are unchanged through 8433c38. C uses custom byte-string buffers/nodes, while Mini uses UTF-16 strings, sealed objects, ArrayLists and managed allocation.

high_confidence_observations: Mini API O3 and Mini CEmitter O3 have identical MK_STATS counters and nearly identical elapsed time.
The strict hand-C O3 implementation is about 1.51x faster than Mini API O3 on the same checksum; the source structure differs, so this includes representation/runtime costs.
The Mini workload performs over 11 million managed object allocations and over 34 million release calls for REPS=5; over two thirds of releases are no-op events.
The sampled API hotpath highlights recursive release/disposal and ArrayList growth/access, not a distinct API-only codegen bottleneck.
analysis.follow_up_proposal: Prioritize managed allocation and release traffic in JSON-like object/collection lifetimes (especially recursive collection disposal and ArrayList growth). Use a structurally matched optimized C variant or allocation-site profiling before selecting a specific compiler/runtime change; current C/API equality indicates switching codegen backend is not a useful lever for this gap.
